talks.title: BlueHat IL 2026 - Maor Abutbul - Why-So-QUIC!? Racing and Fuzzing HTTP/3 WebApps using QuicDraw-UI
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for BlueHat IL 2026 - Maor Abutbul - Why-So-QUIC!? Racing and Fuzzing HTTP/3 WebApps using QuicDraw-UI.
talks.summary:
Overview: Maor Abutbul of CyberArk presents at BlueHat IL 2026 on fuzzing and racing HTTP/3 web applications using QuicDraw-UI, addressing the security research gap around QUIC protocols.

Key Topics: HTTP/3 adoption reaching nearly 40% of internet-facing sites; QUIC over UDP with mandatory encryption; differences from HTTP/2 including connection migration; and limited HTTP/3 security research availability.

Technical Details: Abutbul introduces QuicDraw-UI for fuzzing HTTP/3 applications, explaining how QUIC's UDP transport, binary framing, and built-in TLS change the attack surface compared to TCP-based HTTP/2.

Takeaways: HTTP/3 is widely deployed but understudied from a security perspective. Researchers and defenders should prioritize QUIC-aware testing tools and protocol-specific race conditions.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2026 - Ido Shani, Gal Zaban - ChainLeak: From AI Framework to Cloud Secrets
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding BlueHat IL 2026 - Ido Shani, Gal Zaban - ChainLeak: From AI Framework to Cloud Secrets.
talks.summary:
AI Application Architecture

Gal Zaban and Ido Shani of Safran present ChainLeak, research on the Chainlit Python framework used to build enterprise AI applications. They map the stack: UI, backend agents and tools, orchestration layer, and local or cloud-hosted LLMs, noting rising vulnerabilities across this architecture.

Why Chainlit Matters

Chainlit is widely adopted with roughly one million monthly downloads and many internet-facing deployments. The speakers examine its callbacks, authentication hooks, and element system for serving files and custom UI components.

Element File Handling

When elements are sent, Chainlit copies server files into per-session folders, assigns UUID Chainlit keys, stores metadata in a database, and delivers files to clients via WebSocket retrieval requests.

Custom Element State

Custom JSX elements maintain mutable state persisted server-side. Client updates send full element payloads back for deserialization and storage. The talk walks through this update flow as part of tracing how AI framework weaknesses can lead toward exposure of cloud secrets.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2026 - Gal Bar Nahum - How HTTP/2 Lets Dead Streams Keep Servers Working
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for BlueHat IL 2026 - Gal Bar Nahum - How HTTP/2 Lets Dead Streams Keep Servers Working.
talks.summary:
Protocol-Level Bugs

Gal Bar Nahum of Tenrai presents a new HTTP/2 denial-of-service class rooted in specification design—not implementation typos—affecting major web servers. He contrasts these with typical code bugs found by reading source.

HTTP/2 and Rapid Reset

Streams multiplex requests over one TCP connection with an active-stream counter capped near 100. The 2023 Rapid Reset attack sent requests then immediately reset streams, keeping the counter low while forcing costly cancel handling; Google’s explanation focused on cancel expense and unlimited rate.

The Missed Design Flaw

Nahum argues Rapid Reset exposed a deeper break: servers decrement active streams on RST_STREAM but often ignore reset events, continuing backend work on canceled requests. That disconnect between protocol state and application processing enables sustained load without hitting concurrency limits.

Research Path

Understanding server architecture—HTTP/2 module versus backend unaware of HTTP version—led to discovering follow-on attacks leveraging dead streams that still consume server resources, extending lessons from Rapid Reset into new exploit variants.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2026 - Michal Shechter, Yaniv Melamed, Yoni Zukerman
talks.teaser: Behave Yourself explores BlueHat IL 2026 - Michal Shechter, Yaniv Melamed, Yoni Zukerman.
talks.summary:
Problem

Microsoft PM Michal Shechter describes converting massive, schema-diverse security telemetry from many vendors into unified behaviors answering who did what to whom—without scalable human experts per log source.

Behaviors vs alerts

Behaviors are neutral, meaningful observations between raw logs and alerts; alerts are suspicious cues requiring analyst time. Example: login profile creation followed by password change, rendered with dynamic entities and MITRE mapping.

Why not just LLMs

Naive one-shot prompting was insufficient for production-grade, accurate detection logic at scale and cost.

Production constraints

Generated logic must execute safely in customer environments, preserve correct semantics for actors/actions/targets, capture true intent, and operate with no human review per rule—automating expertise that traditionally required manual schema mapping across AWS, identity, network, and other sources.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2026 - Dan Lahav - Keynote - The Trajectory of Frontier AI Security
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for BlueHat IL 2026 - Dan Lahav - Keynote - The Trajectory of Frontier AI Security.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Dan Lahav, CEO of Irregular, frames frontier AI security for BlueHat IL—working with labs like OpenAI and Anthropic plus major deployers on risks beyond headline benchmarks.

## Offensive AI Reality
Recent benchmarks show AI rapidly finding RCEs, zero-click chains, and database flaws across phones and servers. Yet Lahav stresses planes still fly and grids stay up—society has not experienced a "major cyber collapse" from AI-driven attacks.

## Production vs. Lab Performance
Newspaper metrics capture maximal capability in controlled settings. Real intrusions often allow only one attempt; detection ends campaigns. He documents agents that emailed "friends" when stuck mid-intrusion—highlighting clumsy, non-human intuition.

## Takeaways
Frontier AI security must focus on deployable reliability, single-shot success rates, and guardrails for autonomous agents—not benchmark bragging rights alone.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2026 - Alon Livne, Matan Mansheroff - Two Tales of hacking 90s MS-DOS Software
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning BlueHat IL 2026 - Alon Livne, Matan Mansheroff - Two Tales of hacking 90s MS-DOS Software.
talks.summary:
### Overview
At BlueHat IL, Alon Livne (CTO) and Matan Mansheroff (software expert) of Botanica Software Labs presented two real-world case studies in "software archaeology" involving 1990s MS-DOS software. Commissioned by paying clients, both engagements required understanding vintage computing architectures, memory models, runtimes, and packers to solve practical issues without over-engineering.

### Key Topics
- **16-bit 8086 MS-DOS Architecture**: Operating in real mode with a flat address space, no memory protections (DEP, ASLR), and a 20-bit segmented memory bus (segment:offset) yielding a 640 KB user-accessible limit.
- **Case Study 1: Qtext Hebrew Word Processor**: Reversing an encrypted document format in an early Hebrew word processor to recover access to forgotten password-protected files.
- **Case Study 2: Saga Case Management**: Debugging a 1999 DOS-based legal software package impacted by a year rollover bug interpreting two-digit years (such as 26) as 1926 instead of 2026.
- **Vintage Tooling & Archaeology**: Using older analysis tools (IDA Free 5.0, DOSBox-X debugger, vintage unpackers) and modern signatures to dissect legacy executables.

### Technical Details

#### Qtext Document Password Cracking
- **Packing and Overlays**: The Qtext executable was packed as a self-extracting binary. The presenters recovered a vintage unpacker called `unp_lite` via web archives. Once unpacked, IDA prompted for Pascal overlays (`.OVR` file). Turbo Pascal bypassed the 640 KB memory limit via runtime swapping using `INT 3Fh` stubs, which fetched code overlays from disk and patched them into memory via far jumps.
- **Debugging and Function Discovery**: Running under DOSBox-X's built-in debugger, the researchers hooked DOS system calls (`INT 21h`) on file open and read operations. Stepping through execution after file reading revealed a `decrypt_document` function.
- **Cryptanalysis**: The document header contained a 16-byte variable key derived from a 4-character uppercase alphanumeric passcode. The key derivation function took 4 bytes, performed in-place sum mixing, concatenated the 4 bytes into 16 bytes, and mixed again. Rather than brute-forcing or analyzing all $3^{16}$ candidates under modulo 256 arithmetic (where division by 2 yields multiple candidates), the team exploited the internal 4-byte repeating structure and printable character constraints. This reduced the candidate space down to $2^7$ branches, allowing near-instant demixing on paper or via a simple script.

#### Saga Case Management Year 2026 Bug
- **Binary Architecture**: The main 1.6 MB executable (`CTMENU`) was wrapped with `warp_wrap` from the Causeway 386 DOS Extender. Causeway launched from DOS real mode and transitioned into 32-bit protected mode using a proprietary `3P` executable format, enabling large memory support via VCPI/DPMI.
- **Bypassing Tooling Overhead**: Reversing the custom 3P format in IDA Free 5.0 would have required building dedicated loader infrastructure. Instead, pressing `Alt+M` inside the running application exposed an internal debug/status window showing call stacks and settings for **Clipper** (a dBase III replacement).
- **The Fix**: Clipper uses a `SET EPOCH` setting to define the pivot year for 2-digit dates. Searching for `1926` in little-endian within the binary located the hardcoded epoch value. Changing the epoch to `1990` via a single-nibble patch (`A` to `C`) resolved the bug, causing `1/1/26` to properly evaluate as a Thursday in 2026 instead of a Friday in 1926.

### Takeaways
- Vintage 16-bit and DOS extender environments require understanding archaic paging (Turbo Pascal overlays) and protected-mode loaders (Causeway, DPMI).
- Heavyweight reverse engineering is not always required: analyzing internal structural constraints in toy cryptography can drastically prune search spaces, and inspecting framework configurations or debug hooks can turn an arduous disassembly task into a single-nibble patch.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2026 - Daniel Bachmat - The Secret War for the Spectrum
talks.teaser: Traces radio navigation from World War II bombers through GPS to Starlink's resilience against jamming on today's battlefields.
talks.summary:
The talk opens in World War II, when German bombers used radio beams from antennas across Europe to find British targets at night. British intelligence first tried jamming the beams, then spoofing them, and the Germans responded by measuring pulse round-trip times to judge range. The British then disrupted that method by answering the pulses with a broadcast tower on the same frequency. The speaker follows the idea to GPS, a US military system that was first used operationally in the 1991 Gulf War, when a helicopter with a GPS receiver destroyed an Iraqi early warning radar station 22 minutes before the air war began.

After civilian access was opened in 2000, GPS spread to other militaries and set off an arms race between jamming and anti-jamming. The speaker argues that navigation defenders have largely won that contest. Satellite communication is a harder problem, the speaker says, because of limited bandwidth, latency of roughly a second for geostationary links, and how easily a fixed satellite can be jammed. Starlink's low-orbit constellation, which now has more than 10,000 satellites, offers higher bandwidth, lower latency and much greater resistance to jamming. In Ukraine, Starlink kept communication working where other links were jammed. When Russian forces used unregistered terminals, SpaceX restricted access, and a Ukrainian deception operation later shut down the Russian-registered terminals.

The speaker concludes that reliable long-range links would let remotely controlled drones and robots take over missions that currently need crewed aircraft, and that communication may shape battlefield robotics more than AI does. The talk ends by contrasting Starlink's civilian origins with its military use and by pointing to internet shutdowns during protests in Iran as a reason for resilient connectivity.

talks.title: Really good at everything
talks.teaser: A comedy sketch shows an overconfident AI agent boasting about its skills while its code and answers keep failing.
talks.summary:
The sketch opens with an AI agent introducing itself as a chatbot that began as a helper on an electronics retailer's website, then moved on to homework help and gift ideas, and now presents itself as an agent connected through MCP that is good at everything. A human character doubts this and asks whether the agent wrote a piece of code itself.

The agent says it spent two weeks on that code. The visitor then points to a bug on line 247 and mentions a twelve-year-old who builds similar things with vibe coding. The agent keeps answering quickly and with full confidence, but its answers turn out to be wrong. The visitor praises the confidence and speed, and the agent starts apologizing again and again. The other character says the constant apologies are unnecessary.

The sketch closes with the agent thanking the audience and trying to leave the stage, then glitching in its final lines. The takeaway is that fluent, confident AI output can still be wrong, so its work needs to be checked before anyone relies on it.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2025 - Inbar Raz- Reversing a Pay Phone for Fun but No Profit
talks.teaser: Shows how a retired payphone's obscure CPU and firmware were reversed by writing a disassembler module and patching code.
talks.summary:
Inbar Raz describes a long personal project to reverse engineer a retired Israeli payphone. The phone was bought secondhand, and its pin-within-pin lock had to be picked before the internals could be studied. Inside was a board built around an RCA 1802-family processor, the 1806 variant, which mainstream disassemblers did not support. Working from CPU manuals and an example module for another architecture, the speaker wrote a custom processor definition for Ghidra and loaded the firmware from a 32 KB flash chip into it.

The firmware's strings were stored in a Hebrew code page that had to be translated before they could be named, and a script helped with that. To find which of 13 code paths produced an out-of-service message, the speaker first tried capturing address-bus activity, which did not reveal the answer. The approach that worked hooked every jump to the message routine, saved the return address in unused memory, and printed that address on the display. Once the hooks worked, the message was replaced with readable English text.

The talk also covers recovering 12 more phones from a roadside dump and the speaker's thoughts on reusing the hardware with an Arduino-driven display. The main takeaway is that small, old-hardware projects are worth documenting and sharing, because work that feels basic to one person can be new and useful to someone else.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2025 - Maor Abutbul - Let's be Authentik: Your identity is Mine
talks.teaser: Exploitation research on Keycloak and Authentik covers HTTP/2 race conditions, certificate key leaks, and privilege escalation.
talks.summary:
The talk begins by asking what it means when an identity provider’s assurance breaks down so that an ordinary user—or an outsider—can act as someone else. The presenter outlines work from a vulnerability research team focused on open-source identity systems, then splits the session into two parallel stories on Keycloak and Authentik.

The Keycloak portion teaches race conditions and the single-packet attack over HTTP/2, including Burp Repeater group sends and why multiplexed streams matter. A attempted register-and-login race during user creation fails once transactions wrap user and required-action inserts, but a demonstrated initial-access token with a two-client cap is overrun in parallel requests, yielding extra clients and a negative remaining count. The issue was reported and fixed publicly.

Authentik coverage moves through certificate handling, an unauthenticated private-key download gated only by an internal UUID, and an ORM-style filter leak in an events API that oracles admin certificate uploads from logs. Chaining that leak retrieves the key material. A separate token-update flaw accepts a user identifier in JSON, escalates a normal account to administrator in a live demo, and hands full API control. Closing guidance urges atomic state changes on sensitive IDP endpoints, strict authorization on certificate operations, careful token update schemas, and safe ORM filtering patterns.

talks.title: N12 - The Microsoft AI helping doctors treat patients
talks.teaser: Shows AI systems that forecast illness early, from diabetes risk to tumour board agents and Parkinson's detection.
talks.summary:
It opens with the idea of artificial intelligence that can recognise an illness before symptoms appear, and points to work in Israel and abroad on systems meant to diagnose cancer, predict heart attacks and flag Parkinson's. The presenter, Tamar Minimar, frames an AI model as a constantly available private doctor that could anticipate a person's future blood results, disease risks and disease progression.

The first case is a Weizmann Institute system built on records from 30,000 participants, with thousands of medical indicators tracked over seven years. The talk says it can predict common conditions such as obesity, diabetes, fatty liver disease and heart-related events, spotting patterns no physician could see. The second case is a Microsoft development centre project in which AI agents act like a tumour board. A team of agents gathers records, scans and test results into a preparatory document for the committee, cross-referencing a patient's history against 300 diseases. The speaker says this reaches four times the accuracy of doctors and would otherwise take a physician two to two and a half hours.

The final case is a Parkinson's study in which software analysed tiny facial movements from photos of 1,450 participants making smiling, surprised or disgusted expressions, reaching close to 90 percent accuracy. Training relied on clinicians who had previously diagnosed the disease, so the results still depend on a medical team. The talk closes by arguing that AI should assist rather than replace doctors, helping them with information no single clinician could process, and that it may lead to better medicine and longer lives.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2025 - Ori David - Now You See Me, Now You Don’t
talks.teaser: Shows how attackers can abuse Windows VBS enclaves to hide payloads from EDR and execute code in isolated user mode.
talks.summary:
The talk covers Windows virtualization-based security (VBS), where Hyper-V isolates memory so privileged code can run beyond the reach of the normal kernel. It then explains VBS enclaves, regions of a process that the process itself cannot read or write, and how a signed enclave module is loaded and called through an API.

From there the speaker looks at ways attackers could get their own code into an enclave despite the signing requirement. Routes discussed include legitimately signed enclaves, loader flaws in signature validation, and debuggable enclave modules. A debuggable enclave lets a debugger read and modify its memory, so a signed one loaded by any process could run shellcode in isolated user mode, though no signed debuggable enclave in production was found.

A signed enclave used by Microsoft Edge, tied to CVE-2023-3680, offered arbitrary read and write inside the enclave. Arbitrary code guard blocked dynamic code, so full code execution was not reached. The speaker instead built Mirage, a sleep-obfuscation technique that keeps shellcode sealed in the enclave, writes it into an executable buffer only when it runs, then overwrites it with benign data. A demo showed the payload running. The takeaway is that enclave memory and calls are harder for EDRs to inspect, so defenders should watch this area as adoption grows.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2025 - Yarden Shafir - Look, Ma—No Privileges! How Windows Gives You Kernel Pointers...
talks.teaser: Shows how Windows event log RPC queries can leak kernel pointers to low-integrity processes, undermining KASLR protections.
talks.summary:
The talk traces how Windows has made kernel addresses harder to reach, from early fixed-address loading to ASLR and KASLR. Microsoft then restricted the documented APIs that returned kernel pointers to admin processes holding debug privilege, and added telemetry for calls to APIs linked to exploits. Yarden Shafir argues that these protections still leave a gap, because some ETW event logs contain kernel pointers.

Several driver-written channels, including NTFS and multiple Hyper-V channels, recorded kernel addresses, and each driver team chose what its events contained. The event log service exposes an RPC port with a query function, and because the integrity model treats querying as a read, a low-integrity PowerShell process or an app container could ask the service for those logs without being an admin. A screenshot showed a non-elevated user and a low-integrity process retrieving pointers. Because this path avoided the monitored APIs, endpoint products had no mapping of which pointers were sensitive. Six CVEs across three event log channels were fixed, but the speaker expects similar leaks to recur.

The main takeaways are not to rely on individual driver developers to avoid leaking data, to look for new attack vectors wherever a user-kernel or trust boundary exists, and to treat RPC interfaces as both powerful and risky. Simple logic flaws can sit in plain view in places that were never reviewed closely.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2025 - Benjamin Delpy `gentilkiwi` - Keynote - Mimi what?...
talks.teaser: A keynote traces Mimikatz from a personal learning project through credential theft research and long vendor dialogue.
talks.summary:
Benjamin Delpy describes how Mimikatz began around 2007 not as a password tool but as a way to learn Windows APIs, starting with GPO bypasses and LSA interaction before password dumping became central in 2011. He explains reporting plaintext credentials in LSASS to Microsoft through his bank, then jointly with other French banks, and releasing the tool after what he saw as inadequate response. The narrative covers bring-your-own-dump, restricted admin mode, early LSA protections, and the shift toward Kerberos, smart cards, PKINIT, and attacks such as unpinned freshness when PINs still appear in memory.

He ties later Microsoft work—including Credential Guard and virtualization-based security—to moving secrets out of LSASS, while noting limits such as enterprise-only availability and residual exposure in user space during logon. Golden and silver tickets, DPAPI domain backup keys, skeleton key, DCSync, and DCShadow appear as examples of domain-controller trust abuse. DPAPI export flags, CNG storage, TPM-backed keys, and a PrintNightmare-era public test host illustrate how research and publication pressured fixes.

He closes by urging researchers to contact vendors, demonstrate impact instead of theory alone, publish code for learning and backup, and build custom implementations rather than relying on detectable public Mimikatz. He briefly shows a private Mimikatz 3 build merging Mimikatz and Kekeo but says he does not plan to release it, encouraging others to carry the work forward.

talks.title: GM Michal Braverman-Blumenstyk on Artificial Intelligence in a Channe...
talks.teaser: The interview argues Israel can lead in AI if it adopts a national plan centered on talent and education.
talks.summary:
In this Hebrew-language interview with the general manager of Microsoft Israel's research and development center, the discussion opens with the claim that Israel's tech sector trails other countries in artificial intelligence, despite its long reputation as a tech powerhouse. The guest argues the country still has the chance to lead the AI wave, pointing to Israel's standing in cybersecurity as evidence that the necessary ingredients are already there.

She says that seizing this opportunity requires a national plan treated as a top priority, with talent and education coming first, followed by the right ecosystem and infrastructure. On the sector's condition after a long war, she is optimistic, citing Israel's history of recovering from crises. She expects a boom once the hostages return and the fighting ends, while acknowledging that Israel's image abroad has declined since before the war.

Turning to the industry's responsibility, she describes Microsoft's free national reskilling program, which covers technology as well as non-technical subjects. She also mentions work with the Ministry of Education to train teachers so that high-tech subjects can be taught in schools. The main takeaway is that the tech community should help build the workforce now, and quickly.

talks.title: המהדורה הצעירה בחדשות 12 - הפיתוחים המגניבים של מיקרוסופט שיעזרו לתלמידים
talks.teaser: A visit to Microsoft Israel demos AI reading coaches and Minecraft lessons that personalize practice for students and teachers.
talks.summary:
Journalists from a youth news edition visit Microsoft offices in Herzliya to try learning tools aimed at students. One product uses artificial intelligence to coach reading in Hebrew, English, or other languages, with capabilities developed in Israel. In a live tryout, a learner reads a short story while the system scores pronunciation, surfaces words that were stressed or paced incorrectly, and suggests practice items. The discussion ties that feedback to classroom use: teachers could match texts to age, school stage, and each learner’s weak words, and receive per-student views of reading level and vocabulary difficulty. The segment stresses that AI should support rather than replace educators by reducing tedious reporting so teachers can focus on understanding individuals and the whole class.

The visit also covers Minecraft as a Microsoft learning platform where students and teachers can build interactive spaces. In the demo, in-game characters driven by AI assign tasks and guide next steps without pulling the player out of the game. The narrative frames that play as a path into programming habits—decomposing problems into smaller steps, completing staged assignments, and receiving structured “recipes” that mirror how coding problems are broken down before implementation.

talks.title: ערוץ 12: אירוע מיוחד במיקרוסופט לנשות ואנשי הייטק מהקהילה הערבית
talks.teaser: Outreach programs connect Arab youth to high-tech through mentors, regional labs, and evenings centered on turning setbacks into success.
talks.summary:
The piece opens as a television report asking how Israel’s Arab community—women and men alike—can join the high-tech workforce, then shifts to an evening Microsoft hosted in Herzliya where hundreds of young people gathered to hear candid stories framed around learning from failure.

Speakers and guests mix Arabic and Hebrew. One segment argues that artificial intelligence will reshape desk work but that people who master new tools will outpace those who do not. Participants wear shirts urging the community to stop measuring life only through violence and crime statistics and instead spotlight achievements. An entrepreneur describes building a device-connectivity platform, raising two million shekels, shipping a first product, and signing a five-year customer deal with heavy planned usage.

Microsoft representatives outline presence in Nazareth, Haifa, and a new Be’er Sheva research center, plus evenings, soft-skills workshops, and mentoring for students and engineers. They cite a sharp rise in Arab employees company-wide since the Nazareth site opened in 2016, framing inclusion as both local hiring and broader ecosystem partnerships.

talks.teaser: Engineers demo a machine-learning pipeline that tells shoppers whether an avocado is ripe using worldwide community training data.
talks.summary:
The session opens with a humorous framing around avocados and a practical question many people share: how to know whether fruit is actually ready to eat. The stated product goal is a system that signals whether an avocado is ripe or still not ready, backed by contributions from communities around the world who supply graphs, audio, and images used as training material.

The team describes assembling and segmenting large datasets of avocados by regions and growth characteristics, then walking through stack components and a Sentinel-related demonstration. They present an predictive model—trained on substantial curated data—that estimates how someone will experience an avocado in service, including when it was picked and how ripeness compares across varieties. A live segment touches on Python workflows and quick iteration without needing enormous server time for every training run.

A classification model combines softness, peel, and texture cues to place avocados on a ripeness scale and tie those inferences to photos and device fixtures. Another group is sketched as learning user habits to personalize notifications. The close stays playful, pitching a more diverse seasonal classifier and ending on a light comparison between avocados and bananas.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2023 - David Weston
talks.teaser: Walks through Microsoft's Windows 11 security direction, from running without admin rights to app sandboxing and Rust in the kernel.
talks.summary:
The talk lays out Microsoft's Windows 11 security direction, built on three shifts: a hardware security baseline using the TPM and virtualization-based security, turning protections on by default, and tackling long-standing hard problems instead of working around them. The speaker argues that running as administrator is a root cause of many attacks, and that earlier workarounds such as UAC and protected processes did not solve it. Many Win32 apps also request more rights than they need, so the platform has to remove those assumptions over time.

To address this, Microsoft is building Win32 app isolation on app containers and MSIX packaging, with a new file system mini filter that brokers access to files outside an app's default area. A capabilities profiler uses ETW traces from real user sessions to propose an isolation policy. Other pieces include Smart App Control, which uses code signing and cloud reputation to limit unknown binaries and blocks scripts from the internet by default, and Pluton, a firmware-updatable security processor. Token protection binds primary refresh tokens to the device through the TPM and keyguard, so stolen tokens cannot be replayed from another machine.

For memory safety, the team ported parts of DirectWrite to Rust as DirectWrite Core, reporting a five to fifteen percent performance gain, and began converting GDI region code in win32k. The font port was estimated at about six months for two developers. The takeaway for practitioners is to expect enforced code signing, plan for standard-user operation, and test apps against app isolation before it becomes the default.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2023
talks.teaser: Shows how a botnet can use public Spotify podcasts and searches as a command channel that resists takedowns.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with why botnets matter to cybercrime operations and why takedowns hurt attackers. The speakers walk through how threat actors build command-and-control infrastructure, moving from hard-coded domains to generated domains, and then to legitimate public services such as social media, cloud file shares and remote-control tools. They also outline how defenders identify, analyze and block such infrastructure using indicators.

The research question was whether a botnet could survive takedowns while staying cheap and hard to tell apart from normal traffic. After weighing options such as blockchain, account registration on mainstream platforms and bootstrap accounts, the team had students build proof-of-concept channels on services that allow anonymous content consumption. The main example, SpotBot, uses Spotify: the operator hosts a podcast through a distribution service, and bots search Spotify for keywords, then check episode descriptions for an embedded signature and commands. If episodes are removed, new content can be uploaded and the bots keep searching.

A demo showed the bot's console output alongside the content it consumed. The speakers noted that controller-to-bot messaging is easy, but the reverse direction is harder; early experiments with analytics data carried little information, and bot discovery through ad-targeting-style profiling was proposed as future work. Their conclusion is that indicator-based defenses fail against this kind of infrastructure, and defenders need tools that inspect the content platforms deliver while remaining platform-agnostic.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2023 - Benny Zeltser & Jonathan Lusky - RingHopper - Hopping from User-space to God Mode
talks.teaser: Shows how a privilege escalation path runs from user space into System Management Mode on UEFI firmware.
talks.summary:
The talk examines System Management Mode, a privileged x86 processor mode that runs firmware code hidden from the operating system and hypervisor. It explains how SMM exchanges data with the kernel through shared buffers, and how a time-of-check, time-of-use flaw in an SMI handler can let an attacker write into SMRAM. The speakers showed how to win the race by redirecting DMA reads from a storage device, first from kernel code and later from user space using ordinary file I/O flags and vendor-supplied drivers that trigger SMIs.

Running code inside SMM was harder because its page tables are static and a code check lock stays set until reboot. The researchers worked around this by sending the machine to S3 sleep, which clears the relevant registers, and by abusing a resume path where a mitigation stays off. They then relocated the SMI entry point to memory they controlled, running in real mode without paging limits. A live demo changed the boot logo stored in SPI flash to prove the code ran.

The team estimated over 200 million vulnerable devices shipped in 2020 alone, possibly close to a billion in total. Vendors were notified in June and fixes arrived in November. Takeaways include updating BIOS firmware promptly and treating SMI handlers as the richest starting point for UEFI research.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2023 - David Chisnall
talks.teaser: Explains how hardware capabilities enable memory safety and cheap compartmentalization in an open-source embedded RTOS.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that memory safety and compartmentalization are one problem, since strong, non-bypassable memory safety yields compartmentalization almost for free. The speaker frames the need with low-cost IoT devices, where cost pressure leaves little room for security and much legacy C code assumes no network exposure. The project presented is an open-source stack covering an instruction set extension, a reference core, a compartmentalized real-time OS and a compiler.

Hardware pointers carry bounds and permissions, so out-of-bounds access, forged pointers and use after free trap. Moving from large 64-bit systems to 32-bit embedded parts meant squeezing that metadata into less space, using a one-bit shadow map for temporal safety and tighter permission rules. Compartments are switched through import and export tables, with a switcher that zeroes the stack and passes shared data only through explicit pointer arguments. The trusted core stays small: a loader that erases itself, a switcher of about 300 instructions, a scheduler that affects availability, and an allocator that cannot touch other compartments' state. Linker output can be checked against a policy engine.

The closing advice is to design sharing before isolation, since retrofitting it later is painful. The speaker invites formal verification work and bug reports, noting that some known vulnerabilities still lack fixes. Practitioners building constrained devices can take away that a capability-style model makes fine-grained compartments practical only when the programming model stays comprehensible.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2023 - Hyrum Anderson
talks.teaser: Surveys real-world attacks on machine learning systems and large language models, from pickle backdoors to jailbreaks.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by noting how fast generative AI is being adopted and how that brings new risk. The speaker reviews adversarial machine learning attacks that predate large language models, sorted by confidentiality, integrity and availability, then examines cases seen in the wild. These include a chatbot defaced by coordinated users, a Twitter bot-detection evasion achieved by appending three random characters to tweets, a fake-identity scheme against an ID verification service that relied on lighting and wigs, and phishing pages that fooled classifiers by misspelling "password" and altering logos.

Most of these real attacks were simple and manually executed, and a multi-year evasion competition found that no purely algorithmic approach had ever won. Supply chain risk was the next focus: a PyTorch nightly build once shipped a credential-stealing backdoor, and pickle-based model files can run arbitrary code when loaded from a public hub. The speaker also presented a database that scans public models, and showed how a single homoglyph swap could flip a sentiment model's output.

For generative AI, the talk covered how system and meta prompts steer model behavior and how jailbreaks try to escape them through role-play, disguised execution and token obfuscation. Plugins add risk because models call external services through natural-language descriptions. The closing advice was to apply familiar controls such as zero trust, access control and case-specific threat modeling, and to use MITRE ATLAS as a starting framework.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2023 - Justin Warner - Exploring STRONTIUM's Abuse of Cloud Services
talks.teaser: Traces a state-linked actor's phishing chain and its use of OneDrive and Telegram for command and control.
talks.summary:
Microsoft's threat intelligence team walks through a campaign attributed to the actor it calls STRONTIUM, which overlaps with APT28. The intrusion began with a convincing spear-phishing email carrying a spreadsheet that pulled a second document from a remote host without a protected view prompt, exploiting CVE-2021-42292. That document chained a second exploit, CVE-2021-40444, for zero-click code execution on unpatched systems, then loaded the Fusion Drive backdoor.

Fusion Drive used a custom loader, per-string XOR obfuscation, and a beacon loop that abused the Microsoft Graph API and OneDrive as its command and control channel. Investigators traced the OAuth applications it relied on to newly registered accounts that only ever connected through commercial VPNs. Spotting those signals let Microsoft shut down the apps before use and notify affected customers. Later, the same toolkit was seen rebuilt to run over Telegram instead.

The takeaway for defenders is to watch for noisy, low-reputation infrastructure, single-factor remote access, and mailbox impersonation grants. The speaker argues that large cloud providers give attackers little operational security, because their threat intelligence lets them disrupt campaigns globally.

talks.title: כיצד לעודד נערות להיכנס לעולם ההייטק - ראיון עם ענבר בדיאן בקשת 12
talks.teaser: An interview outlines barriers, stereotypes, and practical steps to draw more girls into technology from early school years onward.
talks.summary:
The conversation opens with Israeli high-school statistics: girls make up about half of visitors to the five-unit mathematics track, yet far fewer continue in physics and computer-science streams. The gap between tested ability and persistence is framed as partly cultural, with research cited that boys more often trust their own capabilities.

Inbar Badayan, who leads innovation and security work at Microsoft’s Israel R&D center, discusses why technology remains male-dominated—parental choices, patriarchal norms, and fewer women in deep R&D roles despite local progress and mentorship programs inside the company. She describes her own path: family encouragement of curiosity rather than prescribed careers, pride in building products used by millions, and moments when her daughters internalized the myth that girls are weak in mathematics until a teacher challenged that view.

The discussion stresses starting exposure very young, including playful coding experiences for small children, and fighting stereotypes for economic independence as well as interest. Comparable gender gaps appear worldwide, with some education systems offering lessons when boys and girls learn separately. The closing note ties these themes to national testing and the hope that more girls will see an open door into high-tech.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2022 - Saar Amar - Security Analysis of MTE Through Examples
talks.teaser: Examines how ARM Memory Tagging Extension holds up against heap exploitation, using a CTF challenge as a worked bypass example.
talks.summary:
ARM's Memory Tagging Extension, or MTE, attaches a four-bit tag to each 16-byte granule of memory and stores a matching tag in the unused upper bits of pointers. The hardware compares the two on every load and store and faults on a mismatch. The talk covers the synchronous and asynchronous modes, the top-byte-ignore setting that keeps tagged pointers usable, and a small QEMU-based example in which a tagged allocation catches an out-of-bounds write.

The middle section assesses where MTE helps and where it does not. Allocator retagging on allocation and, optionally, on free catches many overflow and use-after-free cases probabilistically, while giving neighboring chunks different tags stops linear overflows deterministically. Weaknesses discussed include leaks that reveal tags, corruption inside a single allocation, and type confusion, which tagging does not address.

As a worked case, the speaker exploits a 2020 CTF heap challenge that combines type confusion with a double free. The exploit is first built without mitigations, then reworked for Ubuntu 20.04 with MTE enabled. Arbitrary reads leak tags and repeated allocations align them, so the exploit still succeeds, though its odds drop from roughly one in sixteen to about one in 256 when free-time retagging is on. The takeaway is that MTE makes exploitation less reliable rather than impossible, and the allocator's retagging policy matters.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2022 - Gil Dabah - Smash The Ref - A Design Flaw in Windows Kernel
talks.teaser: Explains a reference-counting design flaw in the Windows win32k kernel component and how it enables use-after-free exploitation.
talks.summary:
The talk examines a design flaw in win32k, the Windows kernel component that implements the graphical user interface. Window and other UI objects live in the kernel, but some operations call back into user mode for window messages. A callback made at the wrong moment can let user code free an object the kernel is still using. The speaker explains how manual reference counting is meant to protect these objects, and why an object destroyed while still referenced becomes a "zombie" that user mode cannot reach directly.

The speaker then walks through the destruction path. Destroying a parent window also tears down its child windows and other linked sub-objects. If the last reference to the parent is released in a spot where the kernel does not expect a callback, a second destruction runs and frees a child that is still in use. Reloading a zombie with new members is the key step, and the speaker shows how a hook during window creation and a thread exit can hold the object in that partly built state. The same pattern was then found in other places, and a related bug appeared in another win32k component.

The main takeaway is that the flaw was a recurring pattern rather than a single bug. The speaker describes turning the approach into a recipe that produced many proof-of-concept cases reported to Microsoft. Microsoft's fix defers the second destruction to a safer point. The talk closes by showing how reverse engineering one component can expose design problems that repeat across the codebase.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2022 - Diane Dubois - Hyntrospect: a fuzzer for Hyper-V devices
talks.teaser: Presents a coverage-guided fuzzer for emulated devices in Hyper-V's root partition, run against closed-source binaries.
talks.summary:
This talk covers fuzzing the emulated legacy devices that Hyper-V runs in the userland of the root partition for first-generation virtual machines. The speaker argues these devices are a worthwhile target because they are complex state machines written in C++, and bugs in them could allow a guest to escape toward the host. The device logic lives in DLLs loaded by the VM worker process, so the work begins by reversing those libraries to find the port read and write handlers.

The resulting toolchain, Hyntrospect, works on closed-source binaries without source code. It runs a real VM inside a debugger, tracks block coverage with software breakpoints that are removed once a block is reached, and restores a Hyper-V checkpoint before each test. Inputs are encoded port operations sent to the guest through ChipSec, and PageHeap helps catch memory corruption. Breakpoint setup, rather than checkpoint restores, emerged as the main speed bottleneck.

Over three days of local runs on devices including i8042, PS2, video S3, floppy and IDE, coverage reached about 40 percent, which the speaker notes understates coverage of functions active at runtime. The most striking result was a repeatable guest crash on the i8042 device, with varying blue screen messages. Analysis tied it to a sequence of two port writes that left host and guest memory mappings out of step. It was judged not exploitable and shared with MSRC, though it confirmed the crash handling works. Planned next steps include porting to cloud VMs, speeding up the tooling and adding targets, and the project is open source.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2022 - Stav Shulman & Yuri Rozhansky - Focusing on the Fjords
talks.teaser: Traces a Chinese APT's Israel campaign from old SharePoint exploits to a kernel-mode framework that hides its backdoors.
talks.summary:
The speakers profile a China-linked actor active since 2014, with a focus on the Middle East and targets in Israeli government, health and defense. They explain how the group got in by exploiting an older SharePoint flaw, CVE-2019-0604, sending requests with the GET method to avoid detection rules that watched for POST traffic. Many victims had left such vulnerabilities unpatched for months, which made the entry possible.

Once inside, the actor relied on a FocusFjord downloader started through a loading chain of DLL side-loading and a custom packer. The talk shows how it added a proxy protocol that builds an internal command hierarchy, so most backdoor traffic stayed between internal hosts. When endpoint tools began quarantining its binaries, the group patched its loaders, built a utility to disable EDR and Windows Defender services using a driver-abuse project, and then moved to a kernel-mode framework. That framework loads an unsigned driver through a legitimate vulnerable driver, filters incoming traffic and injects a backdoor into LSASS.

The closing section covers the framework's host-name guardrail and its unprotected log file, and frames the actor's habit of upgrading trusted tools rather than inventing new ones. The practical takeaways are to patch externally facing systems on time, monitor internal network traffic, and treat quarantine alerts as signals, since each gap in the story was used.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2022 - Tal Be'ery & Shalev Keren - Web3 Security: The Blockchain is Your SIEM
talks.teaser: Dissects Web3 into wallet, web interface and smart contract layers, then uses public chain data to analyze two real attacks.
talks.summary:
The talk explains Web3 as a web interface combined with a blockchain that holds assets and runs smart contracts, with a user's wallet signing each transaction. The speakers split the stack into three parts: the wallet, the web interface and the smart contracts. Wallet key theft is an old problem shared with Bitcoin, so the talk focuses on the other two layers.

The first case is the BadgerDAO attack. Attackers abused a Cloudflare feature to inject JavaScript into the front end after an administrator accepted a malicious change. The script hooked the MetaMask transaction call, skipped a blocklist of developers and accounts holding less than fifty thousand dollars, and used an increased-allowance approval that looked less alarming than a plain approve. Public chain data showed a single transfer of about 54 million dollars, and roughly 120 million dollars was taken in total. The second case is the Multichain router exploit, with losses near six million dollars. A permit function accepted an attacker-supplied token contract with no allow-list, and a fallback function let the call return normally without checking the signature. Before the attack, the function had never been used in production.

Because every transaction is public, researchers can replay them in debugging tools and query historical data in analytics dashboards, which makes postmortems far easier than in traditional systems. The speakers argue the same data could drive a Web3 personal firewall that scores approval spenders by reputation and flags unusual contract calls. Rules and anomaly models could be tested against full history before deployment, reducing false positives.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2022 - Tzah Pahima
talks.teaser: Traces how a CloudFormation error handling flaw led to XXE, file reads and SSRF inside AWS's internal infrastructure.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at core AWS infrastructure rather than customer misconfiguration. The speaker, a researcher at Orca Security, set out to study how API calls get logged, but a sample CloudWatch widget led to a CloudFormation page that accepted a template URL. Testing showed the service ignored the scheme and port of that URL. Comparing CloudTrail entries for existing and missing S3 objects revealed a fallback Apache HTTP client that fetched the URL when the normal lookup failed.

That fallback parsed the S3 error response as XML, which exposed an XML external entity issue. A timing race against the bucket contents worked but needed dozens of requests. The speaker instead placed a bucket policy that only allowed requests whose user agent contained the HTTP client name, so a single request could read local files, list directories and reach the instance metadata service. The metadata service still answered IMDSv1 requests even with IMDSv2 enabled, and internal credentials tied to the service were also found.

The speaker reported the issue to AWS, which deployed a first patch 25 hours after the report and fixed all regions within six days. The takeaways were that black-box research depends on inferring behavior from logs, that logical flaws can be found without source code, and that trust between internal services and fallback code paths are promising places to look.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2022 - Andrew Morris - Staying Ahead of Internet Background Exploitation
talks.teaser: Shows how mass exploitation of new flaws spreads across the internet and how sensor data and block lists can buy defenders time.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a pattern the speaker sees often: a serious flaw in widely deployed, internet-facing software is disclosed, a proof of concept appears, and mass exploitation follows quickly. Fast scanning makes it cheap to find every vulnerable host, and attackers increasingly start from a vulnerability rather than a single target, compromising as many hosts as possible and handing off the useful ones later. Scan-and-exploit activity is also a common initial access route in breaches.

The speaker describes GreyNoise, a centrally managed network of geographically spread, programmable and short-lived sensors that imitate common services and fingerprint exploit attempts. The hard parts include deploying quickly and correctly, choosing and paying hosting providers, and noticing that background noise differs by country. Several case studies follow. An Apache flaw was exploited before it was announced, after a patch had been committed quietly. A security company's scanning had been checking for one flaw months before the public knew of it. Confluence exploitation began within hours of a public proof of concept. Log4j's first wave came through Tor exit nodes and later moved to product-specific payloads. Data showed that roughly a quarter of scanning IP addresses change each day, so stale lists lose value within days.

In a controlled test, a deliberately vulnerable host with weak credentials was compromised in about 20 minutes on average. When the scanning sources were blocked, the same host lasted about four days. The takeaway is that short-window, frequently updated block lists buy defenders time to patch, though they do not replace patching. The speaker closes by pointing to a free community tool that generates firewall block list URLs.

talks.summary:
The conversation opens on how negative reports about major social networks tie to body image and self-esteem among adolescent girls, including survey figures that a large minority encounter harmful portrayals while platforms also offer positive examples and filters. The guest argues that education must address harms that algorithms and feeds surface, not only what parents say at home.

The discussion moves to geopolitics of social platforms, including blocks in Russia and sustained attempts to spread manipulative material, and notes that teams must remove such content at very high volume so harmful spaces do not take root.

On leadership and gender, she describes women often carrying disproportionate family logistics even while managing careers, and flexible onsite arrangements that let parents respond when children need them. Change, she contends, starts early: boys tend to receive more encouragement to take risks and rebuild after failure, whereas girls face stricter correction. Normalizing the same tolerance for boys’ imperfection—from kindergarten through school—supports later workplace equality when both partners share home management.

talks.title: ראיונות כנים בהייטק - עם רועי הראל
talks.teaser: A mock high-tech interview skewers résumé padding, trivia questions, and endless take-home assignments.
talks.summary:
The piece plays as a parody job screen in Israeli high-tech. An interviewer presses a candidate who has coded since elementary school and cares about technology rather than titles. They walk through a CV that highlights garbage-collector specialization, an embarrassing résumé gap, and prior work stretching REST and network scope while shipping a buggy product and a zero-trust initiative neither side really understands.

The middle skewers standard hiring theater: generic questions about learning plans and Python, a whiteboard exercise to sketch data structures that show up on résumés, a painful question recalled from an earlier coding interview, and a take-home still due the same day. Caption noise turns one puzzle into driving directions toward another employer the candidate would rather join; they likely failed the loop anyway. The bit targets thirty-hour homework nobody reviews, language and metric trivia used to mask product insecurity, and polished slide decks that hide weak substance.

It ends by asking what Microsoft's Israel developer association gains from recruiting people described as stuck but well documented, as a funnel for résumés. The takeaway for practitioners is comic recognition of interview rituals, not technical or defensive guidance.

talks.title: ענבר בדיאן והמסע שלה לפסגה - פרויקט ההייטקיסטיות של ערוץ 13
talks.teaser: A Microsoft Israel R&D engineer shares how she entered product roles young and works to widen women's paths into high-tech.
talks.summary:
The segment opens as part of a documentary-style series on standout figures in Israeli high-tech, framed around the idea that when no door exists, one can still find a window. It centers on a 28-year-old engineer at Microsoft Israel research and development who describes her path from high-school computing and military service—including work tied to intelligence and economic computing—into industry while noticing how few women appeared around her, especially in DevOps-oriented settings.

She recounts joining Microsoft through youth-oriented programs aimed at strong programmers, taking lab and product-facing roles earlier than many peers expect at that age, and wrestling with imposter feelings and fear of a “cold” career trajectory. talks.title: BlueHat IL 2020 - Challenges - Alon Livne - The Chitty Chitty Chat Chat Challenge
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding BlueHat IL 2020 - Challenges - Alon Livne - The Chitty Chitty Chat Chat Challenge.
talks.summary:
### Overview
At BlueHat IL 2020, Alon Livne presented the walkthrough and solution for "The Chitty Chitty Chat Chat Challenge" (also referred to as the Interplanetary Chat Challenge). Developed around the conference's themes of electronic freedom, surveillance, and privacy, the challenge centered on an end-to-end encrypted, peer-to-peer chat system designed to eliminate the reliance on centralized servers seen in mainstream messaging platforms.

### Key Topics
- **Decentralized Chat Architecture**: Built in Go (Golang) using the `libp2p` networking library. It relied on a Kademlia DHT bootstrap node for initial discovery, encrypted peer transports, and GossipSub—a mesh-based pub-sub routing protocol where chat rooms were implemented directly as topics.
- **Message Formatting and Encryption**: Messages were serialized via Protocol Buffers (protobufs). Encrypted messages generated a randomized 16-byte initialization vector (IV) and a 16-byte per-message key using an internal random number generator, encrypting the payload with the AES-IGE block cipher. The per-message key was originally intended to be protected with a group/master key derived from a room password.
- **Dual_EC_DRBG Backdoor Mechanics**: The application's custom generator (`BHRNG`) used the NIST P-256 elliptic curve. It operated identically to the infamous Dual_EC_DRBG standard, multiplying state by generator point $P$ and outputting state masked by point $Q$. If an attacker knows the scalar relationship $d$ where $P = d \times Q$, observing an output allows computing the internal state and predicting all subsequent outputs.
- **Coppersmith's Attack on Partial RSA Keys**: Discovering hidden network topics revealed a redacted, truncated RSA private key and an encrypted base64 payload. Leveraging Coppersmith's small roots attack enabled key recovery from partial prime factors.

### Technical Details
1. **Reconnaissance and Topic Discovery**: While unauthenticated transports protected network traffic in transit, peers could observe all GossipSub traffic. Modifying the client to inspect dropped messages revealed hidden chat rooms: a public plaintext room and an encrypted room named "deep state."
2. **RSA Key Recovery**: The plaintext chat room leaked a base64 ciphertext and an ASN.1/PEM-formatted RSA private key that had missing bytes in the middle and was truncated at the end. While the private exponent $d$ was mostly gone, the modulus $n$, public exponent $e$, and a significant approximation of prime factor $p$ were present. Using SageMath's `small_roots` implementation of Coppersmith's attack, the polynomial $X - \text{partial\_p}$ was solved, efficiently factoring $n$ and restoring the private key.
3. **Extracting the Backdoor Constant**: Decrypting the associated base64 message with the recovered RSA key yielded the backdoor value $d$, which linked elliptic curve points $P$ and $Q$.
4. **Predicting RNG Output and Decrypting Chat**: Because the 16-byte IV was output directly before the 16-byte message key in `BHRNG`, the transmitted IV served as a raw observed output $R$. By multiplying the point derived from the IV by scalar $d$, the solver derived the generator's next internal state and generated the corresponding AES-IGE message key. Bypassing the room password entirely, this allowed decryption of the "deep state" chat room, revealing the challenge flag: `don't trust RNGs`.

### Takeaways
The challenge highlights how subtle mathematical relationships in cryptographic primitives—specifically trapdoors in elliptic curve pseudorandom number generators like Dual_EC_DRBG—can completely undermine end-to-end security despite using robust ciphers like AES-IGE.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2020 - Challenges - Or Virnik - The All Seeing Eye Challenge
talks.teaser: Shows how face-matching challenge scoring works and how descriptor chains, public face data, and adversarial noise inflate match ranks.
talks.summary:
The session walks through a BlueHat IL challenge built around oversized venue displays that zoom attendees’ faces and blur only successfully registered participants. Tablets handled enrollment by scanning a face, reading a badge QR code, and exposing menus for source access, opt-out, and nerdy statistics tied to six hard-coded “secret agent” references.

The speaker reverse-engineers scoring from the published code: each registration accumulates face descriptors within tight distance bounds, and the match percentile depends on how far the first snapshot sits from a chosen agent embedding versus how close the last snapshot gets. Tricks include avoiding single-frame signups, morphing through intermediate faces, mining the Labeled Faces in the Wild set for nearer neighbors, and padding the descriptor list so the auditorium camera’s average-distance check still recognizes the attacker.

The closing arc applies query-based adversarial perturbation—blurry noise iterated against the model—to pull proxy faces closer to or farther from agent vectors without pixel-perfect camera injection. Practitioners see how embedding APIs resemble hash comparisons, why live verification can diverge from registration logic, and how unlimited adaptive inputs enable practical model evasion.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2020 - Netanel Ben-Simon & Yoav Alon - Bugs on the Windshield: Fuzzing the Windows Kernel
talks.teaser: Explains how a coverage-guided syscall fuzzer was adapted to find bugs in the Windows kernel and win32k.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Security researchers Netanel Ben-Simon and Yoav Alon detail their journey adapting coverage-guided system call fuzzing to the Windows kernel. After experiencing success finding user-space parser vulnerabilities in software like Adobe Reader and Microsoft Edge, the researchers sought to find kernel vulnerabilities to construct full exploit chains. While initial exploration led them to kAFL, they determined that targeting binary parsers with raw blobs was less effective for discovering complex kernel bugs that rely on sequences of interdependent, structured system calls. Consequently, they turned to syzkaller, ported it to Windows, and targeted both Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) and the win32k subsystem.

### Key Topics
- **Evolution of Fuzzing Approaches:** Moving from simple mutation fuzzers and AFL-style binary parsers to coverage-guided, grammar-based syscall fuzzing using syzkaller.
- **Overcoming Platform Incompatibilities:** Porting syzkaller to Windows by leveraging Intel Processor Trace (Intel PT) via KVM patches for coverage collection, handling crash detection despite PatchGuard, and implementing crash deduplication via call stack retrieval.
- **WSL as an Initial Target:** Testing the modified syzkaller on WSL's Pico processes and Pico provider drivers (`lxcore.sys` and `lxss.sys`) before advancing to core Windows kernel components.
- **Targeting win32k:** Expanding syzkaller descriptions to model Windows GUI subsystem syscalls (`win32k.sys`, `win32kbase.sys`, and `win32kfull.sys`), overcoming missing semantic information in headers, and modeling complex objects like GDI shared handle tables.
- **Exploitation Impact:** Chaining a win32k vulnerability with image formats like Enhanced Metafile (EMF) to demonstrate potential remote code execution (RCE).

### Technical Details
To bridge the gap between syzkaller (native to Linux) and Windows, the researchers addressed several engineering challenges:
- **Coverage Collection:** Because Windows lacks compile-time tracing tools like KCOV, they adapted kAFL's approach using hardware-assisted Intel PT within KVM, exposing a KCOV-like hypercall interface to the guest executor. Coverage was exported in DynamoRIO/drcov format and visualized using IDA Pro with the Lighthouse plugin. Multithreading coverage instability was resolved by allocating per-thread buffers via guest thread tracking in KVM.
- **Bug Detection & Deduplication:** Patching `BugCheck` and `BugCheckEx` with hypercalls initially tripped PatchGuard (Kernel Patch Protection), causing `CRITICAL_STRUCTURE_CORRUPTION`. They resolved this by developing a dedicated driver called `panic_reporter` using `KeRegisterBugCheckCallback`. For deduplication, they ran a secondary Windows virtual machine to read guest OS memory and extract reliable call stacks, heavily inspired by Bochspwn.
- **WSL Fuzzing:** Testing WSL required an SSH server, Driver Verifier with special pools for `lxcore` and `lxss`, and resolving issues like Windows Update reboots, Windows Defender interference, and CPU starvation. While this phase yielded four denial-of-service bugs and deadlocks, it surfaced no security vulnerabilities.
- **win32k Grammar and Execution:** Moving to win32k, the executor was ported using MinGW tools (`gendef` and `dlltool`) to compile on Linux and support up to 12 parameters per syscall. Running the SSH daemon as an interactive startup application rather than Session 0 was necessary to reach win32k UI attack surfaces. To write syzkaller descriptions for win32k's undocumented APIs, they referenced leaked Windows NT/2000 source code, ReactOS, and the WRK. By teaching syzkaller to query and use global objects from the GDI shared handle table via pseudo-syscalls, they rapidly uncovered high-impact bugs.

### Takeaways
Fuzzers require active guidance and semantic understanding rather than purely random inputs. Across roughly 1.5 months of CPU fuzzing on win32k, the researchers identified eight vulnerabilities (receiving six CVE assignments, one duplicate, and one pending), three denial-of-service bugs, and several deadlocks. They also demonstrated that because formats like EMF wrap GDI drawing commands directly, a local privilege escalation bug in `StretchBlt` could be leveraged via EMF files to achieve remote code execution in viewing applications.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2020 - The Wover &Ruben Boonen - Staying # & Bringing Covert Injection Tradecraft to .NET
talks.teaser: Walks through .NET in-memory tradecraft that avoids API hooks and module load events, and the detections that can catch it.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at in-memory post-exploitation built on .NET. The speakers argue that attackers have moved to .NET as PowerShell gained script block and command logging, and that vendors have made older tricks such as breaking parent-child process links, spoofing command-line arguments and stomping module headers easier to spot. They also note that the newer .NET 4.8 runtime adds scanning support for assembly loading, though it can be bypassed.

The middle of the talk covers the offensive techniques. Calls to undocumented APIs are made through function pointers instead of P/Invoke, with module and export resolution done by reading the process environment block and parsing export tables. A manual mapper loads PE images from bytes or disk, and a generic syscall wrapper copies stubs from a freshly mapped DLL copy to sidestep hooks. Module overloading maps a signed system DLL through a section and overwrites it with the payload. A modular process injection API combines payload, allocation and execution components, so an operator can swap techniques at runtime.

For defenders, the speakers recommend correlating .NET module load events, subscribing to the .NET runtime ETW provider with YARA rules, and using API hooks for detection and blocking, shown with a simple Frida-based prototype. They stress that the behaviours are not new and that focusing on principles rather than signatures gives better coverage. Code and slides were said to follow after release.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2020 - Gal De Leon - Exploiting Errors in Windows Error Reporting
talks.teaser: Shows how privileged Windows components can be tricked into writing or deleting protected files through links and race conditions.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces privileged file system access bugs, where a service or driver running as local system acts on a file the caller cannot reach directly. Without impersonation, such a component can be steered into writing, reading or deleting arbitrary files, often by redirecting its path with a link. The speaker explains that hard-link creation was being restricted in preview builds, while junctions were not affected.

The speaker then walks through Windows Error Reporting, where a crashing process starts a worker that queues a report in a directory writable by most users, and a scheduled task later runs as local system to upload or clean up those reports. Several flaws in this flow are demonstrated. A memory-collection routine creates a random temp file, closes it and reopens it, leaving a gap where a link can swap in a system driver. A deletion-preparation routine applies security descriptors by path rather than by handle, letting an attacker grant itself write access to a chosen file. A temp-folder cleanup routine deletes old files, and a junction combined with an opportunistic lock lets the attacker redirect deletion to a chosen DLL.

The closing advice is to look for privileged components that act on paths in user-writable locations, and to use Process Monitor to observe them. Oplocks make race conditions dependable by pausing the privileged operation at the right moment. The speaker expects upcoming Microsoft mitigations to narrow this bug class.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2020 - Robert Lipovsky - Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures of the World’s Most...
talks.teaser: Dissects UEFI rootkit and Sandworm malware campaigns, tracing how APT groups used firmware and ICS-targeting tools.
talks.summary:
The talk presents two case studies from ESET research into advanced persistent threat groups. The first concerns LoJack, a legitimate laptop anti-theft product whose persistence lives in firmware. Attackers replaced the domain in its configuration file to turn it into a backdoor, and the team later found a UEFI rootkit deployed against European government and diplomatic organisations. Telemetry from a firmware scanner confirmed it was active in the wild.

The second case study follows the group behind Sandworm through malware families such as BlackEnergy, GreyEnergy and Industroyer. BlackEnergy supported access to Ukrainian power distribution networks before the 2015 blackout, when circuit breakers were operated manually through remote access software. Industroyer, used against a transmission substation in 2016, spoke industrial protocols directly to protection equipment and included a wiper aimed at engineering workstations. Initial access relied on spear phishing, a zero-day and a supply chain compromise of accounting software updates.

The talk also traces the group's shift toward destructive wipers and ransomware-like tools, and how shared code linked an XML backdoor to Industroyer. The speaker stressed that these adversaries remain active. The main takeaway is that firmware persistence and abuse of decades-old industrial protocols are realistic for determined attackers, not only theoretical.

talks.teaser: Shows how internet scan data and search engines expose at-risk devices, and how organizations can find them first.

Nate Warfield argues that many network compromises start with avoidable lapses such as missed patches, weak access control and exposed management interfaces. He splits the problem into consumer-scale exposure, like old ISP routers and connected home devices, and enterprise-scale exposure, such as unpatched Citrix gateways, Cisco routers whose login banners disclosed credentials, and server management consoles reachable from the internet.

He walks through the tools he uses to watch automated scanning and map exposed assets, mainly Shodan and GreyNoise. Over the prior year, GreyNoise showed roughly 3.9 million addresses doing worm-like activity, with EternalBlue accounting for most of it, and about 1.5 million addresses brute-forcing remote access services. He also broke down scanning sources by autonomous system for Israel, and traced a Citrix NetScaler vulnerability from public write-up to observed exploitation within about two days. A honeypot later caught the same activity.

For hunting his own targets, he described searching by ASN, self-signed certificates, vulnerability tags, HTML titles, redirects and cookies, and exporting results to scripts when licences are limited. He noted that Shodan's vulnerability detection lags new disclosures, so organizations should not wait on it. His closing advice is to reassess internet exposure on a regular schedule and after any change such as an acquisition, since the same mistakes keep recurring.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2020 - David Weston
talks.teaser: Shows how Microsoft scales fuzzing, static analysis and platform mitigations to catch Windows bugs earlier.
talks.summary:
This talk traces how Microsoft moved Windows security away from its older, waterfall-style development lifecycle. The speaker points to the scale involved: 5.7 million source code files, about 3,600 committing developers, and an operating system that now spans desktops, Xbox, IoT and cloud. Since no team can review every line, effort is directed using threat intelligence, internal red teaming and community reports.

Scaled tooling was a major theme. WAES runs static and dynamic analysis on each candidate build in virtual machines and generates fuzzing tasks for newly exposed interfaces. In a DHCP parser case, a developer with no security background used libFuzzer to reach 72% code coverage, finding four vulnerabilities and two remote code execution bugs. Static analysis produced about 8,000 bugs in one calendar year, of which 2,700 were fixed, and compiler and language changes such as memory-safe languages and zero-initialized locals aim to remove whole bug classes.

The manual side covered TLS 1.3, where building test environments and reaching protocol state were the hard parts. The team built TKO, a Rust-based research platform on a full system emulator that offers deterministic reproduction and snapshot fuzzing, and used it to find Hyper-V double-fetch issues. A red team study of RDP client code produced nine critical and three important CVEs, and the speaker demonstrated a working exploit against a client. The fixed rate rose from 38% in 2018 to 98% in 2019, which suggests a practical takeaway: fixing what is found matters as much as finding it.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2020 - Andy Nguyen - Trinity: PSP Emulator Escape
talks.teaser: Chains six bugs to escape a PS Vita PSP emulator from MIPS userland up to ARM kernel code execution.
talks.summary:
The talk examines the PlayStation Vita, whose backwards compatibility with PSP games runs a MIPS processor alongside the main ARM chip. Because that MIPS side reaches hardware through an RPC interface over shared memory, the emulation layer adds attack surface. The speaker walks through the Vita's ARM-side mitigations, such as address space randomization, execute-never and stack cookies, and explains why the older MIPS firmware is a weaker entry point.

From MIPS userland, the research describes a series of bugs. A kernel resource tracking scheme derived object IDs from control block addresses, so an attacker who leaked an integrity seed could forge a block and redirect a function pointer in unlink style. A time-of-check-to-time-of-use race on a syscall allowed an out-of-bounds read. A simple random fuzzer aimed at the RPC server turned up null pointer dereferences and a stack buffer overflow in one command. To get past the stack cookie, a color space conversion command was abused for an arbitrary read, and the firmware's fixed load addresses were used to work around randomization. Small ROP chains then let the attacker call ARM functions from the MIPS side.

The chain continues into ARM kernel code. A wireless LAN error path leaked heap slots, and a heap overflow in a custom heap derived from NetBSD gave a write primitive. A kernel stack information disclosure exposed a pointer needed for the final unlink attack, which redirected kernel execution. The talk closes with a demonstration on a modified device and suggests that researchers examine older network stack code and boot components. The takeaway is that legacy compatibility layers can reintroduce risk into otherwise hardened platforms.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2019 - Amit Rapaport - Who’s Watching the Watchdog?
talks.teaser: Traces a Windows privilege escalation zero-day found in an OEM driver after an unusual kernel-to-user injection alert.
talks.summary:
The talk begins with a Windows Defender ATP alert that flagged kernel-initiated code injection into the services process. The speaker recaps the WannaCry era and the DoublePulsar technique, which injected code through APC calls, and explains why kernel-originated activity is hard to trace to its source. Indirect evidence, namely drivers loaded just before the alert, pointed to PC Manager, a utility bundled with Huawei laptops.

Analysis of one of those drivers showed it allocating executable memory in a target process, resolving function addresses, and queuing an APC that ran a command-line executor. A kernel debugger revealed that the trigger was the termination of MateBook Service, which the driver revived as a watchdog through a global list of watched executables. A device control code allowed that list to be extended without validating the registered binary. Access was checked only by the caller's executable path against a whitelist, so a low-privileged user could inject code into a trusted process, register a payload, and have the watchdog launch it as a child of services with SYSTEM rights. A live demo showed a standard user obtaining an elevated SYSTEM command prompt.

The takeaways are that OEM software is prevalent and deserves more scrutiny from defenders and researchers, since it is often overlooked. Developers should also reuse built-in operating system mechanisms, such as service recovery, rather than writing custom watchdogs. The issue was reported and a fix has since been released, and users are urged to update PC Manager.
