talks.title: BlueHat IL 2019
talks.teaser: Traces how Microsoft's vulnerability landscape has shifted and where exploit mitigation efforts are heading next.
talks.summary:
The talk surveys how the vulnerability landscape has changed, using Microsoft data on bugs fixed through security updates. More vulnerabilities are being fixed, yet fewer are seen exploited within 30 days of a patch, and exploited bugs are increasingly used as zero-days. Attackers have shifted toward social engineering, macros and password spraying, while widespread exploitation of servers, productivity apps and browsers has largely faded as sandboxing and mitigations spread. Memory safety issues still account for about 70% of fixed vulnerabilities, with heap out-of-bounds, use-after-free and type confusion ranking among the top root causes.

The middle section walks through a three-part strategy of removing root causes, disrupting exploit techniques and limiting what a payload can do, along with the challenges in each. Old bug classes persist and developers carry heavy cognitive load, while control flow guard has design limits such as coarse-grained checks. Data-only corruption, such as overwriting a process token, is largely unsolved, and new classes like speculative side channels affect many security boundaries at once. Containment also faces trade-offs between density, performance and isolation.

The closing argument is for reaching a state where vulnerabilities are no longer a significant problem, not zero bugs. Suggested directions include compiler mitigations that remove whole bug classes, such as zeroing structure padding to stop uninitialized memory leaks, using bounds-checked span types in C++, and adopting safer languages where warranted. The speaker also stresses that social engineering and credential attacks need equal attention.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2019 - Andrew "bunnie" Huang - Supply Chain Security: "If I were a Nation State...”
talks.teaser: Surveys how an attacker with large resources could tamper with hardware across the supply chain, from component swaps to implants.
talks.summary:
The talk asks what a well-resourced nation-state could do to attack hardware supply chains. The speaker draws on his own hardware work, including a board whose FPGAs had their markings laser-erased and were returned to production, and memory chips sold as tested parts that were actually untested stock. These cases show that substitution happens even without a security motive, and that a few percent of tampered parts can hide within normal manufacturing defects.

The middle sorts attacks by goal, such as backdoors, exfiltration and sabotage, and by how hard they are to detect. Simple component swaps can change boot straps or RF filters in phones. Implants are harder to find when a die is added inside a package, using wire bonding, through-silicon vias or wafer-level chip-scale packages, which leave little X-ray or visual trace. Other targets include a memory module's SPD chip, ASIC netlists, hard IP blocks and photomask edits that rewire spare cells. Interception points run from couriers and returns to customs and build-to-order fulfillment, where a targeted unit can be selected by its shipping address.

The closing point is that the attack surface is large and porous, commodity packaging technology keeps implants affordable, and build-to-order shipping allows precise targeting. Hardware trust therefore depends on the whole chain of manufacturers, distributors and couriers, not only on the chip itself.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2019 - x0rz - No Code No Crime: UPnP as an Off-the-Shelf Attacker's Toolkit
talks.teaser: Shows how exposed UPnP services on routers let attackers map ports and build a malware-free proxy botnet.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at Universal Plug and Play (UPnP), a set of protocols that lets devices on a network discover each other and open ports on a router without configuration. The speaker walks through the discovery, description and control stages, noting that the control stage uses SOAP without authentication. The starting point is a March 2018 Symantec report on the Inception framework, which reportedly hid behind layers of routers and cloud services.

The central problem is that many routers answer discovery probes from the internet and accept AddPortMapping requests from outside, without checking the internal client address. That allows traffic to be redirected to arbitrary hosts. A small probe run from a VPS found about ten vulnerable routers in 60 seconds. A wider internet scan put UPnP-enabled devices at about 0.5% of the IPv4 space, with around 12% of those vulnerable to the open forward issue, mostly in Southeast Asia. The count was lower in later scans. Chaining port mappings lets traffic hop from router to router, and GetGenericPortMappingEntry exposes active mappings, which helps trace a chain. Calling delete port mapping after a session is established hides the entry from later queries. A separate Akamai-reported campaign used the same flaw to reach Windows machines behind NAT.

The speaker presents these as misconfigurations, so the practical fixes are patching or disabling UPnP on routers and ISP action on exposed devices. Private addresses can be enumerated through the same path, and LAN configuration functions can change DNS settings. With no payload dropped, the activity is hard to log and easy to miss.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2019 - Bhavna Soman
talks.teaser: Transmogrifying Other People's Marketing... analyzes BlueHat IL 2019 - Bhavna Soman.
talks.summary:
The talk tackles a gap in threat intelligence: details of actors, tools and techniques sit in unstructured blogs, white papers and incident reports that analysts must read and connect by hand. The speaker asks whether machine learning can extract those entities and their relationships automatically, producing the actor-to-technique graphs analysts draw today. Off-the-shelf text analytics services were shown to miss APT-specific names entirely.

Training data came from public APT research repositories and about 2,700 documents collected by the team. Labels were produced by matching actor and technique names from a MITRE dataset, which is out of date and made the data noisy, and the corpus was heavily imbalanced. Features combined standard NLP attributes with word2vec embeddings trained on cyber text. Three models were compared: two conditional random field variants, with and without embeddings, and a stacked bidirectional LSTM with dropout to limit overfitting. The LSTM did best on actor recall overall, but on unseen tokens only the CRF with embeddings recalled new entities, so it powered the demo.

The demo tagged an actor and its techniques in report-style text, and malware families in another passage. A phrase like "Fancy Bear" was tagged as an actor only when the surrounding sentence described an attacker, not a teddy bear. Applied to the collected corpus, the approach showed that techniques such as obfuscated PowerShell and process hollowing, often seen as advanced, also appear in commodity malware. Planned work includes attention networks, data augmentation, and better relationship and temporal extraction. The takeaway is that automated extraction can help analysts choose where to place detections.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2019 - Lucas Leong
talks.teaser: Make Static Instrumentation Great Again details BlueHat IL 2019 - Lucas Leong.
talks.summary:
The speaker explains why coverage-guided fuzzing of closed-source Windows binaries is difficult. WinAFL relies on dynamic instrumentation that slows execution, earlier static rewriting tools need full symbols, and hardware-assisted Intel PT approaches struggled inside virtual machines. The speaker built PEAFL, a tool that statically rewrites PE files by duplicating an executable section, inserting coverage code there, appending a section for the coverage bitmap, and repairing headers, relocations and jump targets.

The hardest problem is separating code from data in the executable section when no symbols exist. Misread data gets instrumented and corrupted, while missed code leaves branches pointing at stale addresses. The speaker used a semi-automated approach that validates branch targets and fixes remaining cases by hand. On a GDI+ benchmark in a Windows 10 virtual machine, the rewritten binary ran about twice as fast as under WinAFL, with overhead around double native execution. A demo kernel driver with a planted crash was fuzzed live. Case studies included a kernel driver with an undocumented format, where patching a checksum helped find crashes, a CNG driver that needed valid object headers in its inputs, and registry hive fuzzing across the whole kernel, which required skipping a self-modifying branch.

The talk closes by arguing that static instrumentation delivers speed but is not a clean or reliable approach, with missing symbols as the main obstacle. The same rewriting can feed back more than coverage, such as memory or stack state for finding uninitialized variables, and it applies beyond fuzzing to tracing and bug detection. The speaker said the source code would be released later.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2019
talks.teaser: Shows known and new fault injection attacks that bypass embedded secure boot, and how designers can harden boot chains.
talks.summary:
The talk addresses why secure boot remains vulnerable on embedded devices, and aims to give guidance to the people who design its hardware, its software and the products that ship with it. The speakers review public breaks first. One is a bootrom downgrade that replaced a strong signature check with a weak hash that contains no secrets. Another is a buffer overflow in a USB recovery mode that could be exploited with ordinary software techniques. The rest are fault injection bypasses of hash and length checks on a game console and a handheld. They note that many boot implementations lack basic exploit mitigations and that the attack surface is often larger than assumed.

They then present attacks they describe as new. The first targets one-time programmable memory. Its configuration flags are copied into shadow registers by hardware before the CPU leaves reset, so a glitch during that transfer can flip a secure boot enable bit before any code runs. The second shows that encrypting the second-stage bootloader does not stop a glitch attack. A plaintext payload is laid out with a sled of pointers, and a glitch that corrupts a load during the copy can send the program counter into the injected image, skipping decryption and verification without a key. A live demonstration on an STM32 target, driven by a fault injector and a Python framework, reported around 260 successful bypasses in about an hour over roughly 9,000 experiments.

For practitioners, the takeaways are to keep boot designs simple, limit the algorithm choices an attacker can pick, and authenticate code and data before using them. Designers should drop privileges where feasible, make fixes possible in the field, and block rollback to vulnerable versions. Fault effects are hard to predict from paper reviews, so the speakers recommend testing hardware directly with fault injection as part of a secure development lifecycle.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2019 - Or Pinchasof - Bridging Emulation and the Real World with the Nintendo Game Boy
talks.teaser: Shows how a Game Boy Advance link protocol was sniffed, reverse engineered and emulated to trade Pokémon with a PC.
talks.summary:
The talk traces a project from around 2005 to connect a Game Boy Advance to a PC, so that Pokémon Ruby and Sapphire could be traded with a version the speaker did not have access to. It starts with the console's two linking modes, multi-pak and single-pak multiboot, and with the physical link cable, whose data lines carry bit-level serial transfers at about 115,200 bits per second. A logic analyzer and an Arduino sniffer captured real transfers, and reading the BIOS and game code against hardware specification documents revealed the multiboot stages: probing, header, a simple key exchange, the data transfer, and a checksum before execution on the slave.

Next, the speaker built an Arduino-based interface that let a PC push code into a second console, then integrated the link logic into the Visual Boy Advance emulator. Trades failed because USB serial latency pushed transfers outside the timing the game expected. Moving the code to a Raspberry Pi with direct GPIO access, dedicating a CPU core to the emulator, and tuning timing and frame throttling reduced the delay to almost nothing. Custom test software run on real hardware was used to compare the emulator's register state and timing against the console.

The live demonstrations were only partly successful: multiplayer loading in single-pak mode worked, but Pokémon trades were sensitive to delay. The main takeaway is that an embedded system like this exposes every layer, from bit timing to game logic, and that newer hardware or interfaces do not always beat older direct port access.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2018 - Daniel Gruss, Moritz Lipp & Michael Schwarz - The Case of Spectre and Meltdown
talks.teaser: Researchers trace Meltdown and Spectre discovery, then explain transient execution attacks and KPTI-style mitigations.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens as a playful “evidence board” investigation into why four independent groups reported Meltdown and Spectre within months of each other. The Graz team and co-presenters map shared history—prefetch attacks, blog posts, Black Hat roommates, Paul Kocher’s earlier timing work, Project Zero, and coincident Rowhammer collaboration—to argue the find was inevitable once microarchitectural side-channel tooling and expertise existed, not a conspiracy.

The technical core uses cooking and documentary analogies to explain CPU caches, out-of-order execution, and speculative execution. Meltdown is shown as transient loads that touch kernel memory before permission checks commit, leak values through flush-and-reload, and motivate Kaiser-style kernel page-table isolation (KPTI) in Linux, Windows, and macOS, with real performance trade-offs on context switches. Spectre variant one abuses trained branch prediction on bounds checks; variant two poisons the branch target buffer for indirect branches. Mitigations such as LFENCE on checks, IBRS, retpolines, and microcode updates are surveyed along with hyperthreading and indirect-branch costs.

The close urges the field to stop treating microarchitectural leakage as out of scope, balance speed with safety the way other industries did, and treat post-2017 devices as security-improving even when raw performance gains flatten.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2018 - Lee Holmes - How to Design a New Cloud Platform with a Strong Security Posture
talks.teaser: Describes how Azure Stack was hardened by default, with sealed hosts, constrained operator access and tightly scoped identities.
talks.summary:
The talk covers how Microsoft designed Azure Stack, a hybrid cloud platform that brings Azure services on-premises for disconnected sites, regulated environments and legacy hardware. Earlier attempts fell short: the Windows Azure Pack relied on lengthy hardening guides that customers might skip, and the Cloud Platform System showed that a validated whole system carries risks its individual components do not.

Design decisions followed from that. Hosts are sealed so customers have no fabric access, secure boot and TPM 2.0 form a hardware root of trust, and the baseline builds on Windows Server features such as credential protection, code integrity and Device Guard. Service credentials rotate daily through group managed service accounts kept out of domain admin groups. Operators use a privileged endpoint whose support access needs a two-phase unlock involving Microsoft, and every session is logged. Network whitelisting at switches, software-defined networking and host firewalls limits lateral movement, while controllers use Just Enough Administration instead of WMI-based admin interfaces.

The closing section covers audit policy and central event collection, a cloud controls matrix assessment, and vendor threat modeling and independent pen tests. One vendor's pen test found flawed firmware and overflow bugs in open-source components, which were fixed upstream. The takeaway is to use built-in platform features, accept the engineering work that hard fixes need, and refuse requests that weaken the design.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2018 - Mathy Vanhoef - KRACKing WPA2 in Practice Using Key Reinstallation Attacks
talks.teaser: Explains how key reinstallation flaws in the WPA2 four-way handshake let attackers decrypt and replay Wi-Fi traffic.
talks.summary:
The talk examines a flaw in WPA2 found in the four-way handshake, the exchange where a client and access point prove they share a password and derive a fresh session key. The speaker explains how that key is then used with a per-frame packet counter, which only stays secure if the counter is never reused under the same key.

The attack tricks a client into reinstalling a key it already holds. An attacker relaying traffic on a rogue channel drops the final handshake message, prompting a retransmitted message three that resets the counter. Reused counters then let captured frames be decrypted and replayed. With CCMP that is the limit, though TKIP and GCMP would also allow forgery. Some implementations were vulnerable and others were not, and a Linux and Android supplicant could be made to install an all-zero key.

The practical advice centers on patching both clients and access points, since patching one leaves the other exposed. Access points can shield unpatched clients by not retransmitting message three. The talk also corrects myths, such as the idea that attackers must be nearby or know the password. It closes with disclosure lessons: formal proofs do not guarantee that code matches its model, and multi-party disclosures should prepare for leaks.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2018 - David Weston - Windows: Hardening with Hardware
talks.teaser: Shows how Windows uses hypervisors, custom hardware and shadow stacks to enforce code integrity, isolation and tamper resistance.
talks.summary:
David Weston, who works on Windows security, argues that the traditional list of security boundaries and the old immutable laws of security no longer match what modern devices must guarantee. He uses the Xbox One X as an example of a device designed to resist unrestricted physical access with custom silicon, and presents it as a model for what a stronger Windows could promise. He then sets out six security promises covering code execution with integrity, protection against credential theft, casual physical access, persistence, least privilege and attestation.

Much of the talk covers how these promises are being pursued. Hypervisor-enforced code integrity uses second-level address translation and mode-based execution control, and kernel control flow guard's bitmap is protected by the hypervisor after a red team showed it could be rewritten. Firmware, especially System Management Mode, is presented as the weakest link, with a security mitigations table for SMM and capsule firmware updates as responses. A software return-address protection was pulled before shipping and replaced with a hardware-backed shadow stack developed with Intel. DMA remapping limits what a device plugged into a Thunderbolt port can reach, and tampering with Defender ATP is addressed by an enclave-based attestation engine that reports changes to the cloud.

The closing section covers container isolation with Krypton, GPU access through the IOMMU, and the Windows 10 S edition. The takeaway for practitioners is that future Windows protections will rely more on hardware, firmware and attestation, and that users can check which of these features are enabled on their own devices.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2018 - Matt Tait - Keynote: Fake News and Info-Ops: Modern Information Warfare…
talks.teaser: Traces information warfare from ancient propaganda and Soviet forgeries to modern leaks, social media floods and deepfakes.
talks.summary:
Matt Tait opens this BlueHat Israel 2018 keynote by arguing that fake news and disinformation are old problems rather than a novelty of 2017. He separates disinformation, which deliberately misleads, from misinformation, which is an honest mistake, and explains why people accept facts that match their existing views. Tribalism and confirmation bias make that worse. He illustrates the pattern with Ramesses II's self-glorifying account of the battle of Kadesh and Octavian's allegedly forged will of Mark Antony, which was used to justify war.

He then moves to the Cold War, citing 1982 congressional testimony that put Soviet active measures at about three billion dollars a year. Forged telegrams in India, Nigeria and Greece were used to stir unrest and mistrust. He then covers modern operations: the 2014 hack of Ukraine's election commission, which published a false winner before officials took the site down, the takeover of the TV5Monde broadcaster, and the DNC leaks, where two releases of the same emails differed in edits, exposing forgery. He also describes WikiLeaks-style daily dumps that flooded the news cycle and divisive issues such as Black Lives Matter, used to split society.

Looking ahead, Tait warns of convincing deepfakes, ransomware that could leak stolen data as pressure, and influence campaigns run by non-state groups. His proposed responses include tamper-proof metadata that reveals edited documents, relying on primary sources rather than asking users to judge truth, reputation-based automated moderation, and social tools that expose people to opposing views.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2018 - Matt Graeber
talks.teaser: Shows how Windows code signing trust can be subverted through validation hijacking and forged certificate chains.
talks.summary:
The talk challenges the habit of trusting anything signed by Microsoft. A notepad.exe loaded from an unexpected directory, with its company name altered, still verified as a Microsoft signature in Autoruns, Explorer and sigcheck. The speaker points out that many signed Microsoft binaries are already known to be abusable, so a valid signature only attests origin and integrity, not benignness.

The first attack hijacks the registry-registered signature validation functions the operating system uses for portable executables. Redirecting the verification entry to an exported ntdll function that always returns true lets a binary carrying a stolen Microsoft signature pass, as seen in the Bad Rabbit case. This needs admin rights. The second attack does not: a standard user can clone a Microsoft certificate chain with a PowerShell cmdlet and import the forged root into the trusted root store, which triggers a prompt that can be automated away, then sign malicious code that looks Microsoft-issued.

For defenders, the talk recommends treating any failed signature check as highly suspicious and monitoring changes to the SIP registry keys. Other indicators include files sharing one authentic code hash across different file hashes, missing timestamps, and certificate chains whose validity periods line up exactly. Validation should key on certificate thumbprints checked against Microsoft's published trusted root list, not on publisher name, which the attacker controls.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2018 - Marina Simakov & Itai Grady
talks.teaser: Shows how attackers abuse Active Directory computer accounts across recon, lateral movement and persistence, while staying hidden.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that attackers concentrate on user and service accounts, while computer accounts get far less monitoring and can still be turned into a powerful foothold in an Active Directory domain. The speakers walk through how these accounts can be abused at each stage of an intrusion. During reconnaissance, an attacker can look for computer accounts that were created with empty passwords by some provisioning tools, either by testing logons or by requesting service tickets and trying to decrypt them. For lateral movement, a compromised computer account can be used to open a secure channel on behalf of a target server, which yields the session key needed to sign traffic and get past SMB signing during relay attacks.

For persistence, the presenters show how a relayed administrative LDAP session can be used to set delegation on a computer account, so that it can request service tickets for other users, including domain administrators, against a chosen service. To avoid detection, they add access control entries that deny read access to the delegation-related attributes, so the account looks ordinary to anyone querying the directory. Because no physical machine is attached, its password never rotates, so the access persists. A live demo runs through the relay, the attribute changes and the hiding step.

For defenders, the mitigations include scanning for computer accounts with empty or weak passwords, monitoring bursts of ticket requests and logon operations from one machine, auditing delegation settings, and marking privileged accounts as sensitive and not delegable. To find objects hidden through access control, the speakers compare results from LSA SID lookups with standard LDAP queries. Their takeaway is that computer accounts belong in the same monitoring scope as privileged user accounts.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2018 - Oran Avraham - eMMC Hacking, Or: How I Fixed Long-Dead Galaxy S3 Phones
talks.teaser: Shows how a faulty eMMC storage chip bricked Galaxy S3 phones and how the speaker recovered them.
talks.summary:
Around 2012, Galaxy S3 phones began failing without warning in a problem called sudden death syndrome. Samsung released a kernel patch in the MMC subsystem, and the speaker studied it to understand the cause. The patch contained a hidden backdoor sequence built from manufacturer-reserved commands, and an odd erase call. Using that backdoor, the speaker dumped the firmware running inside the chip's controller.

Analysis of the dumped firmware showed the root cause. The flash translation layer wrote a miscalculated value into its metadata, and the default exception handler then looped forever, so the chip stopped responding at boot. Samsung's patch avoided triggering the bug rather than fixing it. To recover bricked phones, the speaker used a bootloader flaw reachable over USB, with out-of-bounds read and write bugs left unpatched on the S3. When the boot partition was corrupt, the phone could load the bootloader from an external SD card instead. Interrupting the chip's boot within a 35 millisecond window forced it into its boot ROM, where new firmware could be flashed and the metadata reformatted.

The talk closes with early work on newer eMMC chips, tested on a development board, where a comparable vendor command returned a firmware image. The main takeaway is that eMMC is NAND flash behind a controller with its own firmware, and hidden vendor commands can expose that firmware to recovery and analysis.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2017 - Marina Simakov & Tal Be'ery - The Enemy Within...
talks.teaser: Shows how shared local administrator accounts create hidden lateral movement paths in Windows networks, and how to detect them.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how local Windows accounts, whose password hashes sit in the local SAM database, can be abused during lateral movement. The speakers argue that local authentication gets less attention than domain credentials, and that identical local administrator passwords across domain machines turn a network into one where any compromised host reaches all the others. They also cover risks from local users defined through old group policy preferences and from enabled guest accounts.

The live demo follows an attacker who compromises one domain account and brute-forces a local administrator password with a custom tool that works locally, so it avoids network monitoring. The attacker then dumps the local hashes, queries other machines for their local administrators using ordinary domain-user rights, and runs code remotely with pass-the-hash. On the compromised host, the attacker can also add a backdoor user to the administrators group and strip domain admins of their rights.

For defenders, the speakers present Local Hero, a scanner that runs from a separate machine without installing agents. It collects local users and group memberships remotely and flags dormant accounts that suddenly log on, brute-force indicators, privileged group changes, enabled guest accounts, and cloned accounts that share an exact password-set timestamp. Recommended hardening includes restricting remote SAM queries, denying remote access for local accounts through group policy, and rotating unique local administrator passwords with LAPS.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2017 - Benjamin Delpy 'gentilkiwi' - From Mimikatz to Kekeo
talks.teaser: Traces how Windows exposes credentials in memory and on domain controllers, plus abuses of Kerberos smart card logon.
talks.summary:
Benjamin Delpy, the author of Mimikatz and Kekeo, walks through how Windows has kept authentication secrets in memory since Windows 2000. Early releases stored reversibly encrypted passwords inside the LSA process with the decryption key kept alongside them. Later providers such as WDigest, tspkg and livessp held clear-text or easily recoverable material, and Windows 8 biometric sign-in kept the password in a recoverable vault. He then reviews the Windows 8.1 and 10 mitigations, including LSA protection, Protected Users and Credential Guard, and explains where he thinks each one falls short.

The middle of the talk moves to domain-level abuse. With the right privileges, a tool can ask a domain controller over the directory replication protocol for account hashes, AES keys and the DPAPI domain backup key, without placing a file on the controller. He also covers the older NetLogon NRPC route, skeleton key implants, SID manipulation for escalation, and synchronization data from Azure AD Connect. The replication attack was shown live.

The closing section covers Kerberos with smart cards. Kekeo requests tickets using a PIN and a card through PKINIT with a Diffie-Hellman variant, and he shows that pre-signed requests can be prepared for a later time inside the clock-skew window. He also places a self-issued administrator certificate on a blank smart card that Windows never recorded as issued. For defenders he suggests watching for Diffie-Hellman parameters in PKINIT traffic, protecting the DPAPI backup key, and monitoring replication requests to domain controllers.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2017 - Omer Zohar
talks.teaser: Measures how decoys, traps and beacons catch attackers moving through a simulated enterprise network.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a common case where an attacker has already landed on one workstation inside an organization and must move laterally to reach valuable data. The speaker argues that defenders control their own assets and can use that to lure intruders away from real systems, using decoys (fake hosts that mirror the network) and traps (planted lures on real machines that point to decoys or send a beacon when opened).

To test the approach, the team built a corporate environment with servers, workstations, domain controllers and security tools such as IDS, firewall and SIEM, then ran a month-long capture-the-flag event. More than 50 security professionals tried to find five pieces of data while staying undetected, and 34 malware samples were run against the same network. Among the results, application-based traps were the most frequently found overall, and human attackers touched about ten traps each on average. Malware focused on structured application data such as registry entries. Attackers who used the ARP cache were 40% more likely to later access a decoy. Across the contest, 66% of attackers hit a decoy, and no single decoy service crossed 50%.

The speaker concluded that combining decoys, beacons and traffic analysis caught more attackers than any one method, and that diversity matters because no single trap covers every attacker. Deception widens the knowledge gap between a prepared attacker and an improvised one, pushing intruders into noisy behavior that is easier to detect. Defenders should treat detection as the goal rather than deception itself.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2017 - Prof. Yehuda Lindell - Securing Data-In-Use in the Cloud
talks.teaser: Explores why naive cloud encryption schemes leak sensitive data and what stronger data-in-use approaches can offer.
talks.summary:
Cloud adoption brings operational benefits and often stronger baseline security, but organizations give up direct control and face collateral damage from mega-breaches that have nothing to do with their own mistakes. The speaker frames the harder problem of protecting data while the cloud actually computes on it, contrasting schemes that need no provider changes with those that require modified services.

For the unmodified-cloud setting, deterministic and order-preserving encryption look attractive because search and sorting still work, yet the talk walks through concrete failure modes: frequency analysis, auxiliary information, trivial keyword injection into encrypted mail stores, and published recoveries against real health databases where large fractions of fields were decoded with full certainty. Order-preserving schemes fare worse, including on sparse GPS tracks and intersection samples where plotting ciphertext still exposes structure.

Probabilistic searchable encryption improves snapshot resistance but leaks access patterns that document-injection and known-plaintext studies can exploit, especially in email-like settings. The closing path combines searchable encryption with secure multi-party computation and mix-net style resharing to support richer SQL-style queries at practical cluster cost, while stressing that weak “encryption” can invite misplaced trust in what is safe to move to the cloud.

talks.title: BlueHat IL 2017 - Marion Marschalek - The Binary Whisperer
talks.teaser: Shows a graph-based static analysis tool that flags malware behaviors such as key logging and dynamic API loading.
talks.summary:
Marion Marschalek presents a tool built to answer a practical question for malware analysts: can a binary be queried for its intentions without hours of manual reverse engineering? The talk argues that much new malware is repetitive copied code, that sandboxes rarely trigger a sample's full functionality, and that proving a file is clean is far harder than finding a malicious one. The approach is static. Using radare2, the tool recovers functions, cross-references, Windows API imports and strings, and places them into a call graph.

The middle of the talk covers how that graph is made usable. Thunk pruning shrinks graphs built from Visual Studio binaries, and indirect calls, such as thread and hook handlers, are matched through top-down and bottom-up searches. String list detection and character frequency checks filter out garbage strings. Recurring API patterns, called gadgets, flag behaviors such as dynamic API loading, process and file system iteration, thread creation, a global keyboard hook used as a keylogger, and a system shutdown routine. Case studies show a small graph that reads like a downloader, and a sample that lists antivirus product names. Graph metrics, including the share of disconnected nodes and per-kilobyte counts of API calls and strings, help spot packed or obfuscated code. The speaker also compared packing indicators across a targeted malware set and a random set of samples.

The speaker is open that the tool is a prototype and not ready for production, with graph building taking seconds to about five minutes and gadget queries under a second. The takeaway is that static analysis of malicious software deserves more attention, and that tracking metric changes across related binaries can show how code evolves. The code is published on GitHub under the MIT license.

talks.title: Think Next 2016- Raz Izhaki Tamir, CEO and Founder, SkyFi
talks.teaser: Clustered Space Seed nano-satellites expand after launch to deliver gigabit global internet and flexible backhaul from one constellation.
talks.summary:
Large parts of the world still sit outside reliable online connectivity because conventional satellites cost tens to hundreds of millions of dollars to build and launch. The presentation frames global linkage as a shared nervous system and asks whether space can serve as the layer that reaches people on sea, land, and in the air.

The company describes Space Seed nano-satellites launched in clusters on shared rides with larger spacecraft. After deployment, units expand into a full platform with solar panels and a dish, targeting about one gigabit per second per satellite. A constellation on the order of sixty spacecraft is portrayed as enough to cover the planet. Footprint steering, clustering, and machine learning are cited as ways to raise capacity where demand spikes, including toward Israel.

Use cases sketched in the talk include Wi-Fi coverage in Africa, cellular backhaul in the United States, cloud backhaul in Japan, links to aircraft and vessels, and backhaul toward submerged data centers—all from one flexible constellation. The closing message ties connectivity to human stories and ideas rather than hardware alone.

talks.title: Think Next 2016- Jasmin Fisher, Senior Researcher, Microsoft Research
talks.teaser: Shows how executable biology models built like software help predict cancer drug resistance and tailor glioblastoma treatment.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the question of why cancer remains so hard to solve. The speaker explains that cells are complex systems of many interacting molecules, genes and proteins, and that cancer has no fixed plan; it evolves and reacts to genetics and environment. The proposed answer is an approach called executable biology, developed over about twelve years in a Cambridge research group. It treats biological processes as computer programs and applies formal verification, the same kind of checking used for software and hardware, to confirm they behave as intended.

The speaker described how computational models are built to mimic cellular processes and are then compared with laboratory observations, which reveals gaps in what is understood about a mechanism. A graphical, drag-and-drop tool developed at Microsoft Research lets biologists who are not professional programmers build and explore these models. One leukemia model predicted new drug combinations that could overcome drug resistance. In work with a pharmaceutical company, models built from patient-specific clinical data produced predictions that were then checked experimentally on the same patients' cell samples. For glioblastoma, a simulated tumour can test chemotherapy and radiotherapy options in minutes, whereas dish-based testing can take weeks or months.

The main takeaway is that such models can reveal the drivers and bottlenecks of cancer, which might be targeted across different cancer types and used to support personalised treatment. The speaker does not claim cancer will be eradicated outright, but expects that within ten years, using these technologies, the problem will be considered solved.

talks.title: Think Next 2016- Gerald Jay Sanders, CEO, SkyTran Inc.
talks.teaser: Presents SkyTran, an elevated magnetic transport system pitched as a low-cost, low-energy answer to urban traffic congestion.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the argument that traffic is getting worse as car ownership grows in fast-developing regions, and that building more roads only draws more cars onto them. The speaker presents SkyTran, an elevated transport system that runs above surface traffic on a slim guideway held up by a small pole. He claims it costs far less to build and run than light rail or a bullet train, and uses less energy than a hybrid car.

To explain how the vehicle lifts, the speaker runs a hand demonstration with a magnet dropped over a plastic sheet and then over an aluminum one. Over aluminum the magnet slows sharply because induced currents in the metal resist it, which he compares to the braking of a roller coaster. Pairs of angled magnets, which he calls magnetic wings, produce the same effect, and a small glider and a vehicle model rise off the track once pulled forward. Propulsion comes from a rotary magnetic motor inside an aluminum sleeve.

The speaker says the project is a NASA Space Act company based at Ames Research Center, developed with Israel Aerospace Industries. It has moved from subscale models to a full-size demonstration system under construction in Israel, with a test vehicle already running on its guideway. He says the system can reach about 240 km/h, skip stations to follow a set schedule, and that several cities have requested systems.

talks.title: Think Next 2016- Satya Nadella, CEO, Microsoft
talks.teaser: Frames a mobile-first, cloud-first era where conversational assistants and data platforms aim to restore broad productivity growth.
talks.summary:
The opening contrasts a century of steep productivity and living-standard gains with slower progress since the mid-2000s, using that gap to pose whether the next technological wave can match earlier industrial revolutions. From there the talk centers on a platform mission aimed at individual and organizational success across global markets, including Israel’s deep participation in the vendor ecosystem.

The middle section outlines three long-term bets: rethinking productivity around scarce attention and conversation-centric work, illustrated by staged demos where a digital assistant assembles calendar, profile, document, CRM, and news context for a sales meeting and later ties wearable health data to personal goals. Parallel themes cover hyperscale distributed cloud, data and machine learning as economic currency, and new personal computing form factors from collaboration displays to mixed-reality hardware, with a promotional segment on holographic use cases.

Practitioners hear less about specific defenses than about where compute, intelligence, and user context converge. The close urges widening impact beyond fashionable consumer apps toward healthcare, agriculture, and other sectors so digital surplus spreads more evenly across societies partners touch.

talks.title: Think Next 2016- Yoram Yaacovi, GM, Microsoft Israel R&D Center
talks.teaser: A keynote ties workforce automation to emerging roles, demos submerged cloud infrastructure, and frames cybersecurity hiring growth.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by celebrating twenty-five years of Microsoft research and development in Israel and uses a food-supply analogy: where almost everyone once grew what they ate, today only about four percent of people put food on the world's plates. The speaker extends that pattern to work, citing expectations that around two billion jobs could disappear by 2030 as automation reaches law practice through acquired legal tooling, janitorial work through robots, and driving through autonomous vehicles, while noting U.S. research suggesting widespread autonomy could sharply cut crash rates.

Rather than treating displacement as purely negative, the talk highlights unfamiliar future occupations from analyst literature—augmented-reality space designers, limb fabricators, and others—and points to Microsoft examples. One is a partner-built in-car immersion experience using Cortana when drivers need not watch the road; another is an underwater datacenter trial shown on video, where engineers must send divers when pumps fail, stability returns, and power use sits around twenty-seven kilowatts.

The closing argument is that visions of abundant new work still require trustworthy systems. The speaker cites one billion personal records stolen in a single recent year, steep average breach remediation costs, and a projected gap of two million cybersecurity specialists by 2019, presenting security expertise alongside exotic future roles as career paths listeners might choose.

talks.title: Microsoft Ventures TLV Demoday Batch #7- Axonize
talks.teaser: Pitches an IoT back-end-as-a-service that lets product companies skip building duplicate cloud server stacks.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with a smart electric meter as a familiar example of connected products: a device measures consumption, sends readings to the cloud continuously, and the utility analyzes the data and offers usage guidance. The speaker argues that every IoT offering shares the same three pieces—a device, a user-facing application, and a server linking them—and that the backend patterns are largely identical across industries, centered on ingesting data, monitoring, analyzing, and surfacing business information.

After years building such platforms in multiple companies and segments, the team founded Axonize to deliver that stack as a managed service so customers avoid multi-million-dollar bespoke backend projects and stay focused on devices and apps. The pitch cites Gartner-scale IoT growth and per-device annual backend fees, positions a large addressable market, and highlights early customer work including two Tyco initiatives (industrial irrigation and refrigerated rooms), another project in Jerusalem, and pipeline deals. Partnerships with Microsoft, Cisco, Dell, and Broadcom are mentioned, along with $1.5 million in seed funding, a five-person team, and deep prior platform experience together at Schneider Electric.

For practitioners watching a venture demo, the takeaway is structural rather than technical: commoditized IoT cloud plumbing is treated as a reusable product, with Axonize aiming to be the default server layer for new IoT products.

talks.title: Microsoft Think Next 2015- Michael Arena
talks.teaser: Explores how adaptive space and social networks let bold ideas spread inside large corporations instead of dying in isolated teams.
talks.summary:
The speaker frames a coming transformation in the automotive industry, where software and connectivity matter as much as traditional engineering. General Motors, he argues, must pursue bold bets such as connected vehicles, urban mobility, and autonomy, which makes how ideas move inside the company as important as the technology itself.

Drawing on roughly eight years of interviews with more than four hundred people, he rejects the lone-inventor story and describes two parallel systems inside firms: formal operations needed to scale and local pockets where ideas begin. He introduces adaptive space as the connective layer where ideas link across clusters, sponsors sell concepts into the formal system, and breakthroughs appear at intersections. A centralized innovation group reportedly achieved no adoptions over three years until members dispersed and three innovations reached the market within the next year.

He ties the model to GM work in Israel, semi-autonomous Cadillac Super Cruise experiments, and the FNR autonomous concept car, and describes GM 2020 activities such as orthodoxy challenges, three-minute idea pitches, and twenty-four-hour co-labs. Practitioners hear that most corporate innovation fails without social dynamics, and that deliberately building adaptive space—not eliminating operational structure—unlocks hidden organizational potential.

talks.title: Microsoft Think Next 2015- Yoram Yaacovi
talks.teaser: Wearables, stadium cloud platforms, and camera analytics reshape how fans, officials, coaches, and athletes engage with sport.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by framing how sensors, wearables, and cameras are flooding sport, alongside projections of massive growth in connected devices. Cloud platforms and machine learning are positioned as the layer that can ingest that data and turn it into insights for fans, coaches, officials, and players alike.

Several case studies anchor the middle. A partnership with Real Madrid targets hundreds of millions of distant supporters with a virtual stadium experience tied to Microsoft cloud services. Replay Technologies’ multi-camera 3D views revisit a controversial gymnastics vault final, showing how replay might challenge human scoring. In the NBA, ceiling-mounted analytics illustrate why Steph Curry’s unusually steep three-point release angle correlates with elite accuracy.

The close shifts to personal wearables: the speaker compares step and calorie metrics against peers and against Cristiano Ronaldo, arguing that sport and consumer technology are converging. The practical takeaway for listeners is less about a single product than about where data capture, cloud analysis, and fan or athlete-facing dashboards are heading across the industry.

talks.title: Play My Tone at Think Next 2012
talks.teaser: Shows how Tonify lets users mix cloud music, loops, and effects into personalized ringtones and share them in under thirty seconds.
talks.summary:
The presentation introduces Tonify, described as an intelligent social mobile music mixer for blending favorite tracks into layered mixes in less than thirty seconds, even for unskilled users. The walkthrough covers pulling music from the cloud or a personal library, browsing popular and highly rated tracks, and searching by artist, album, or song title.

On a chosen track, the app extracts idea loops from the full recording and narrows the result to three strong mixing options. After picking a loop, the speaker throws it into the mixer, plays it back, and accepts recommended sound effects. Additional effects and a recorded voice overlay complete the mix, which can be saved as a ringtone and shared on social media; the demo continues on Facebook where the finished mix can be played from the profile.

The speaker explains that Play My Tone began from frustration in traffic when changing a fallen-off iron ringtone took roughly two hours of manual effort. The intended takeaway is that personalized, shareable ringtones should be quick and enjoyable rather than a lengthy chore.
